Selecting the proper kit is kind-of a long topic that requires a write-up to do it correctly (this post isnt nearly long enough imo), as the 'right answer' entirely depends on what you see yourself doing with it (or know what you'll be doing with it).

Popular/reputable brands are (in no particular order): Crye Precision, First Spear, Spiritus Systems, AWS, Velocity Systems, Lindnerhof, Ferro Concepts, LBT Inc., or Eagle Industries. (I'm a buy once, Crye once kind of guy--- but I'd trust any of these brands if you dropped me in D.R. Congo or Yemen or something with them.)

As for plates, it's not uncommon to spend ~1000$ for them. Do not buy some sketchy ass thing you found on Alibaba. Most people consider their lives to be worth more than a thousand bucks. The point of all the gear is to help you do what you need to do and not die doing it. Getting shot in the heart (dead) or having a sucking chest wound is not good imo. Who wants a collapsed lung? Not you! Reputable brands are: Hesco, AT Armor, etc.

The categories below aren't exact, depending on your setup-- any of the ones listed below "can and do" overlap into other categories to some degree.

CARRIERS

Light Carrier options are: Crye LVS, Spiritus Systems LV-119, etc --- These are generally light duty/light utility/plain clothes options.

Light-Standard Carrier options are: Crye JPC, Velocity Mayflower APC, LBT6094, Ferro Slickster, etc --- More serious light duty/light utility

Medium-Standard Carrier options are: Crye AVS, Eagle Industries Aero, First Spear AAC, Lindnerhof Plate Carrier V, etc. --- Standard/combat duty and utility

Heavy-Duty Carrier options are: Crye CAGE Chassis, Eagle Industries CIRAS, etc. --- These are very bulky and not as popular in the civilian market unless you want to RP being a ninja turtle with the the armor.

The Crye JPC is extremely popular (for a reason) but lacks some of the features a standard carrier might have. IMO it's not a bad option to start with and will let you get your feet wet wearing kit (pouches, mags, all that). It's also not bank breaking either, at ~210$.

If you decide you want to upgrade into an AVS or AAC or something down the road, you'll have plenty of reference/experience after using a JPC (or equivalent) to look for the things you want in a carrier.

DO NOT FUCKING BUY CONDOR OR AR500. Those companies are shit and they make shit products. Condor falls apart while sitting on the couch and AR500 tries to sell side armor as chest plates.

HELMETS

You'll need to decide whether you want a bump helmet or a ballistics helmet. Then you'll need to decide whether you want a high-cut/fast helmet or a full helmet. Popular brands for helmets are Team Wendy, Crye, Lancer, 3M, Ops-Core, MTEK, or Hard Head Veterans.

If you're serious about getting kit, you should have a bump helmet at minimum. Try to get in and out of a vehicle a few times as fast as you can without wearing a helmet or running through heavy vegetation. The first time you get fucked up by a tree branch or smash your head into your car somehow, you'll want one for when you really really need it.

For just general helmet and carrier setup knowledge or examples, I would recommend watching Garand Thumb (aka flannel daddy) on Jewtube, since he talks about why he does certain things. Which is valuable to anyone who hasn't run kit before.

PRACTICE

Don't buy kit and not wear it. Wear it around the house, wear it to the range, wear it when you go camping, wear it when you take a shit, wear it when making babies--- get used to being in it and using it. You don't want to find out that you can't shoulder your rifle properly when you really need to one day because some fiddly bit on your rig came loose and you never noticed it before-- BECAUSE YOU DIDNT WEAR YOUR FUCKING KIT AND TRAIN WITH IT.

Ignore anyone who gives you shit over wearing your kit, you do you, because you might be stepping over the bodies of people who died from sucking chest wounds, because they didn't take preparing themselves for a bad day very seriously.

Everyone wants agency, aka the ability to decide and choose what they do, when they do it, for any reason they want to. But most people don't want any responsibility. But if you want agency, you need to take on responsibility too-- which means properly preparing yourself to defend your life or your family's (even if you end up never having to), without having to rely on other people to do it. So recognize that you'll be stepping up to the pump if/when things go bad and WEAR YOUR FUCKING KIT WHEN YOU TRAIN.
